spike_swarm_sim.physics_engines package¶

spike_swarm_sim.physics_engines.base_engine module¶

class spike_swarm_sim.physics_engines.base_engine.BaseEngine(dt=0.02, T_control=0.1)[source]¶

Bases: abc.ABC

Base abstract class of physics and render Engines. Its role in the simulation is to iterate the physic simulations and collision detections of the entities in the environment and render the graphics. Precise engine implementations must inherit from this class, properly overwritting the required abstract methods to cover the engine’s basic functionalities. The implementation can be either supported on an extern physics simulations library or coded from zero.

Parameters

  • dt (float) – time step of the physics simulation (in seconds).

  • T_control (float) – period of the sensing+control+action loop. It cannot be lower than dt and it is set to 5*dt by default. Essentially this means that the physics are updated 5 times in between every executing of sensors, controllers and actuators.

Variables

  • engine (BulletClient) – pybullet client engine.

  • render (bool) – flag indicating if the simulation is run in visual or render mode.

  • connected (bool) – whether the engine is connected or not.

Abstract method for connecting to physics and render engines. Some common actions to be taken, apart from creating the engine client, are to set either visual or direct mode, set up all the physics constants (gravity, sampling period, etc.) or adding all the WorldObjects to the engine.

abstract ray_cast(origin, destination)[source]¶

Abstract method for casting a batch of rays between pairwise coordinates in origin and destination lists and verifies if there is some object/obstacle in between. It returns the id of the first encountered object.

Example:

>>> # Cast two rays, both of them starting at [0,0,0] and with destinations
>>> # [1,0,0] and [1,1,0] respectively.  
>>> origins = [np.array([0,0,0])] * 2
>>> destinations = [np.array([1,0,0]), np.array([1,1,0])]
>>> # The result is a list with 2 components, each storing the id of the first 
>>> # obstacle detected in the ray trajectory (or -1 if no object was detected). 
>>> ids_list = ray_cast(origins, destinations)
Parameters

  • origin (list) – list of numpy arrays with the set of origin coordinates.

  • destination (list) – list of numpy arrays with the set of destination coordinates.

Returns

list of int identifiers of the first intersected WorldObject by each of the casted rays between pairwise origins and destinations. For each ray, if no obstacle was detected it returns a -1.

spike_swarm_sim.physics_engines.pybullet_engine module¶

class spike_swarm_sim.physics_engines.pybullet_engine.PybulletEngine(*args, **kwargs)[source]¶

Bases: spike_swarm_sim.physics_engines.base_engine.BaseEngine

3D Physics and Render Engine class based on the pybullet library. Its role in the simulation is to iterate the 3D physic simulations and collision detections of the entities in the environment and render the 3D graphics.

Parameters

  • dt (float) – time step of the physics simulation (in seconds).

  • T_control (float) – period of the sensing+control+action loop. It cannot be lower than dt and it is set to 5*dt by default. Essentially this means that the physics are updated 5 times in between every executing of sensors, controllers and actuators.

Variables

  • engine (BulletClient) – pybullet client engine.

  • render (bool) – flag indicating if the simulation is run in visual or render mode.

  • connected (bool) – whether the engine is connected or not.

  • physical_sensors (dict) –

    maps sensor reference names to actual physical links of the robot. Specifically, each key of the dict corresponds to a sensor (‘distance_sensor’, ‘light_sensor’, …), which in turn have a subdict as value. The subdict of each sensor has another int key per each of the available sectors (e.g. from 0 to 7). Finally, the value of each sector contains information about the physical link of the corresponding sensor sector (link name, link idx, ghost link, etc.). For example, the value of the sector 0 of the ‘distance sensor’ would be:

    Example:

    >>> print(self.physical_sensors['distance_sensor'][0])
>>>     {'link': 'IR0', 'ghost_link': 'ghost_cone_DS0', 'orientation': array([0.     , 0.     , 0.26179]), 'idx': 33, 'ghost_link_idx': 34}

  • physical_actuators (dict) –

  • luminous_objects (dict) –

  • gui_params (dict) – unused ftm.

connect(objects)[source]¶

Connects to the pybullet based physics and render engines. It starts the pybullet client in either visual or direct mode, sets up all the physics constants (gravity, sampling period, etc.) and adds all the WorldObjects to the engine.

Parameters

objects (iterable) – iterable of WorldObjects whose physics have to be simulated.

disconnect()[source]¶

Disconnects the pybullet based physics and render engines.

step_physics()[source]¶

Iterates all the 3D physics of the world entities using pybullet.

step_render()[source]¶

Iterates the graphics visualization at given FPS.

add_objects(objects)[source]¶

Iteratively add all the WorldObject entities to the engine so that its physics can be taken into account during the simulation.

Parameters

objects (iterable) – iterable of WorldObjects whose physics have to be simulated.

add_physics(obj)[source]¶

Adds the requested entity to the engine so that its physics can be taken into account during the simulation. It uses the pybullet function loadURDF, that creates the pybullet entity described in the form of an URDF file. The precise file describing the entity is an attribute of the corresponding WorldObject class.

Parameters

obj (WorldObject) – entity to be added to the engine.
